sub.en: Look at each sentence. Which half takes will — the one with when, or the other one?

items.q: When I ___ home, I’ll have a shower.
items.why: Same trap as the first conditional: after when / as soon as / before / after / until you use the present, not will.

items.q: As soon as the course ___, I’ll call you.
I’ll pack the bag before I ___ to bed.
We won’t start until everybody ___ here.
After we ___ back, I’ll write it all down.
I ___ you as soon as I arrive.
items.why: The OTHER half is the one that takes will.

items.q: If the weather ___ bad, we’ll stay in the cabin.
items.why: RECYCLED from Lesson 25: the same rule in the if-clause.

items.q: I won’t take my phone. I ___ it for a week. (a prediction about next week)

tts: Hi, I’m calling about the MovNat training course in November. — OK, great. Are you interested in coming on the course?
Yes, I am, but I’ve just got a few questions I’d like to ask. — Right. Fire away.

Well, the first question is, do you need to have a good level of fitness? It’s just that I’m quite unfit at the moment. Does that matter? I mean, do I need to go to the gym before I begin the course? — No, no. The course is for anybody.
And what happens if the weather is bad? — We go out anyway. As soon as you arrive we’ll give you the right clothes.

o: whether you need a good level of fitness

acts.title: Seven days without a signal
text: On Friday we leave for a week in a cabin with no electricity, no signal and, according to the booking email, “a stream”.

I have made a list of what I will do when I get there, which is itself a sign that I need to go. As soon as we arrive I am going to put the phone in the car and leave it there. I won’t take it out until we drive home. Before it goes in the car, I will take one photograph, because I know myself.

The plan after that is simple: walk in the morning, cook slowly, sleep when it gets dark. My doctor has been telling me for two years that gentle exercise and sleep would do more for me than anything she can prescribe, and I have been nodding and doing nothing.
If the weather is bad, we will go out anyway; that is apparently the point. If it is very bad, we will read.

The part I am dreading is Sunday afternoon, when the week will be half over and I will start thinking about Monday. When that happens, I have promised to say it out loud instead of checking a phone that isn’t there.

items.s: The cabin has no electricity and no signal.
She will leave the phone in the car.
She will take the phone out during the week.
She will take one photograph first.
Her doctor has recommended gentle exercise and sleep.
If the weather is bad, they will stay inside.
She expects Sunday afternoon to be difficult.

items.sit: You describe the first thing you will do at home this evening.

If the weather is bad, we stay in.

She says gentle exercise will helps more than pills.

write.q: Write about a week away, or the week after a busy period: 6 sentences. Use when, as soon as, before, after and until once each, plus one first conditional. Remember that the time clause takes the present.
write.model: When I finish this project on Friday, I’ll sleep for about eleven hours. As soon as I wake up, I’ll go for a long walk and take nothing with me. I’ll turn my work email off before I leave the office, not after. I won’t look at it again until Monday morning, and I have told two people so that I can’t quietly change my mind. If the weather is good, I’ll cycle to the lake. After the week is over, I’ll probably say I should do this more often, and then I won’t.

speak.q: Answer out loud: What will you do when you get home today? What will you do as soon as this course finishes? What won’t you do until the weekend?
speak.model: When I get home I’ll cook something properly instead of eating standing up. As soon as this course finishes I’ll take a week off. I won’t open my work email until Monday.
